# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## Rethinking What a Successful Meeting Looks Like

There is a common assumption, woven deep into workplace culture, that a good meeting is one where everyone walks out nodding. We celebrate alignment. We praise teams for being "on the same page." Managers often judge their own effectiveness by how smoothly discussions proceed and how rarely conflict surfaces. Agreement, in this view, is the currency of progress.

But this assumption deserves scrutiny. Agreement can be shallow. It can be performative. It can mask the fact that people understand a situation in fundamentally different ways, or that nobody wants to be the one to voice doubt. A room full of nodding heads may be a room full of people who haven't yet discovered they disagree—or worse, a room full of people who know they disagree but have decided it's safer not to say so.

The alternative is counterintuitive but powerful: a genuinely productive meeting can end not with consensus, but with a precise, shared understanding of what people disagree about, what evidence would settle the matter, and who is responsible for gathering that evidence.
